impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 permits broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies where any member of the claimed genus would be effective, and whether the panel's enablement standard for method claims is consistent with Supreme Court precedent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache using anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies against Eli Lilly's enablement challenge. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding sustains overly broad claims, creates confusion about enablement standards for method claims, and undermines medical innovation. The case has significant implications for the pharmaceutical and biologics industries regarding the permissible scope of method-of-treatment claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims, particularly in biologics, benefit from a more permissive enablement standard that may sustain genus-level claims where functionality across the genus is established.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor pharmaceutical and biotech companies face broader blocking patents on methods of treatment, potentially limiting freedom to operate and increasing licensing costs for new therapeutic antibodies and biologics.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents to the licensee such that the licensee could sue for infringement in its own name without joining the patent owner, and whether the agreement automatically terminated when the licensee shifted its business to enforcement activities.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, granting standing to sue without joining the patent owner. The court also held the agreement did not terminate when the licensee shifted to patent enforcement. This decision clarifies the rights of exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities to maintain infringement suits independently.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clearer standards confirming their right to enforce patents without joining the original patent owner, facilitating patent monetization strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on standing challenges to exclusive licensees, and may face increased patent enforcement activity from non-practicing entities operating under exclusive licenses.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award. The court affirmed the finding of trade secret misappropriation liability against Ford. This case provides significant guidance on trade secret damages methodologies and the interplay between trade secret and contract claims in software licensing disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from broader acceptance of trade secret damages models and reinstatement of jury contract damages awards, strengthening enforcement of IP rights in technology licensing relationships.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal alternatives to licensed software face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk and may face substantial damages exposure under multiple theories including both trade secret and contract claims.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that can yield materially different results for the same material.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that Cocona's patent claims for a waterproof, breathable membrane were invalid as indefinite because the MVTR limitation could be measured using different test methods (upright vs. inverted cup methods) yielding different results, and the specification failed to inform skilled artisans with reasonable certainty which method defined the claim scope. This decision reinforces that claims incorporating measurable parameters must adequately specify the measurement methodology when different methods yield different outcomes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in materials science and manufacturing patent cases can challenge claims with functional measurement limitations where the patent fails to specify the measurement protocol, providing a potent invalidity defense.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims defined by measurable parameters face heightened indefiniteness risk if the specification references multiple testing standards without clearly specifying which governs the claim scope.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly assessed damages including willful infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on patent eligibility under § 101, vacating the summary judgment of eligibility for certain claims of two patents while affirming eligibility for claims of two other patents. The court also affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings, including willfulness. This decision provides important guidance on the boundary between abstract mathematical concepts and patent-eligible technological improvements in communications technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology benefit from the affirmation that claims directed to specific technical implementations of signal processing improvements can survive § 101 challenges, with damages including willful infringement sustained.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry-standard communication protocols face continued patent infringement risk, and the split eligibility ruling creates uncertainty about which claim formulations will survive § 101 challenges in this space.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether wireless communications apparatus claims reciting transmission of electromagnetic signals 'over air' are indefinite, and whether such claims satisfy the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed final judgment of invalidity but on alternative grounds, reversing the district court's indefiniteness ruling while holding the claims invalid for lack of enablement. The court found that while the claims were not indefinite, they failed to enable the full scope of the claimed invention. This decision illustrates the Federal Circuit's willingness to reach alternative invalidity grounds and provides guidance on the relationship between indefiniteness and enablement analyses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative enablement grounds even when reversing the lower court's indefiniteness analysis, providing multiple avenues for invalidating overly broad claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that appellate courts will independently evaluate alternative invalidity theories not relied upon below, potentially invalidating patents on grounds the patentee did not have a full opportunity to address at trial.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) in a Hatch-Waxman ANDA litigation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's patents on crystalline cabozantinib malate salts for cancer treatment satisfy the written description requirement. The decision upholds patent protection for Cabometyx® through 2030 against generic challengers. This ruling reinforces the ability of pharmaceutical companies to obtain valid patent protection on specific salt forms and crystalline polymorphs of active pharmaceutical ingredients.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies benefit from confirmation that patents on specific crystalline salt forms with adequate disclosure survive written description challenges in ANDA litigation, supporting product lifecycle management strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry where brand companies hold patents on specific salt forms, potentially delaying generic competition and maintaining higher drug prices.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the term 'internal diameter' in oil and gas tool patents and whether the jury verdict of infringement and damages was supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's judgment finding direct and induced infringement of an oil and gas tool patent, raising issues about claim construction of the term 'internal diameter.' The case involves significant damages in the energy services industry and the proper interpretation of dimensional terms in mechanical patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in mechanical and energy technology patent cases benefit from rigorous appellate review of claim construction, particularly for dimensional terms that could have multiple reasonable interpretations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the oil and gas industry face the risk of vacated infringement judgments based on claim construction disputes, requiring costly retrials and creating uncertainty in patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract dispute about whether asserted claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, finding the case involved state-law contract interpretation rather than a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for patent settlement agreement disputes and may affect how parties draft contingent payment provisions in patent licenses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that contract interpretation disputes over settlement terms will be heard by regional circuits applying state law, potentially resulting in more predictable outcomes under established contract law principles.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies involved in patent settlement disputes face jurisdictional uncertainty and potential transfer between circuits, increasing litigation costs and creating forum-selection complications in settlement agreement drafting.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying a motion for attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and Rule 11 sanctions where the patent holder filed suit despite § 101 rejections of related patent applications and a prior court finding of ineligibility for a related patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of attorneys' fees and sanctions, holding the district court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that filed infringement claims despite PTO § 101 rejections of related applications and a prior district court invalidation of a related patent on § 101 grounds. This decision signals heightened scrutiny of patent holders who pursue litigation despite substantial indicators of patent ineligibility.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from stronger appellate oversight of fee-shifting decisions, increasing the deterrent effect against pursuit of infringement claims involving patents with significant eligibility concerns.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of fee awards and sanctions when filing suit on patents closely related to those already found ineligible or rejected on § 101 grounds, requiring more rigorous pre-filing assessment.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court, after dismissing a patent case for improper venue, may also reach the merits and dismiss on patent eligibility grounds under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal for both improper venue and patent ineligibility under § 101 for e-commerce bridge computer patent claims. The court held that the district court did not err by addressing the merits of eligibility after finding venue was improper. This decision permits courts to issue merits rulings on patent eligibility even when venue is improper, potentially giving such rulings preclusive effect.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases can obtain merits-based dismissals on § 101 grounds even when venue is improper, potentially creating issue preclusion that prevents the patent holder from re-filing in a proper venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk of adverse eligibility rulings with potential preclusive effect even in improperly venued forums, limiting their ability to refile claims in more favorable jurisdictions.
